extracted.intended_audience: NSF staff, science policymakers, research administrators, and analysts of peer review and research evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical criteria for identifying and evaluating major scientific innovations and for assessing patterns and fairness in peer review and funding (including citation-based utilization measures, expert-panel mentions, and measures of NSF support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of expert mentions as indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the number of mentions by expert panelists (frequency of choices) as an indicator of significance; note that an average of only 6 percent of all items mentioned across all fields received 4 or more mentions and no single item received mentions by all responding panelists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation caveat: low consensus (few unanimous mentions) may reflect a large number of legitimate candidate items and the limited number of choices allowed for panelists, reducing the chance that two judges mention the same item. Thus frequency is informative but must be interpreted in context of panel size and choice limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish once-mentioned vs twice-or-more-mentioned items
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare characteristics of items mentioned only once with those mentioned two or more times to detect significant differences; e.g., chemistry field chosen for such a comparison because of smaller number of items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validation step example: have program officers review once-mentioned items and select those believed to have most significantly advanced the discipline (in the study, program officers chose 47 of 57 once-mentioned chemistry items), then perform the same analyses as for multiply-mentioned items to assess similarity and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of innovation (what counts as innovative research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation consists of contributions to knowledge in science, including discoveries of new things or properties, new instruments to observe nature, new techniques to observe or analyze, or new theories and languages to study and express nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this broad definition when deciding whether a contribution qualifies as an innovation; includes any contribution to the understanding of the nature of the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation as an indicator of utilization
rubrics_metrics.description: A citation to a prior publication is one direct indicator of the use of prior research innovations by subsequent scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats: A citation does not reveal the kind, extent, or significance of the use—it may be perfunctory or ceremonial, positive or negative. Each citation must be examined in the context of the citing article to determine exact use. Empirical generalizations from studies: most citations are positive rather than negative or perfunctory; as citation counts increase over time the likelihood of positive (substantive) use increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly-cited papers as probabilistic indicator of innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly cited articles are usually reports of innovative research; while exact degree of innovation cannot be determined without examination of each paper, statistically a highly cited article has a high likelihood of denoting a significant innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two general claims: (1) All innovative research is highly utilized by the scientific community and usually highly cited for a time; (2) Highly cited papers are innovative to some degree, but the precise degree requires examining individual papers and citation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartile partitioning of papers by accumulated citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition a cohort of papers (e.g., chemistry publications from a year) into four ranked groups by ordering papers by total citations and accumulating papers until each group accounts for roughly one-fourth of the total citations (highly cited, moderately highly cited, moderately cited, low-cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sampling procedure example: sample the four sets on an equal and random basis by selecting a citation from one set, looking up the cited paper, and identifying the funding sponsor (where identified) to estimate proportions of citation-utilization sponsored by different funding sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delineate citing domain to match sponsor mission
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring sponsor 'share' of utilization via citations, delineate the citing domain in close correspondence with the mission of the sponsoring agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the NSF study concentrated on basic research and excluded journals of chemical engineering and applied chemistry; omitting applied-domain journals can understate industrial sponsorship because industry is dominantly applied research. Align domain selection with agency mission to get meaningful sponsor-performance indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure sponsor share of utilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the proportion of citation-utilization (citations to a set of papers) that was sponsored by different funding sources to provide an indicator of agency performance relative to mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example results: for chemistry-citing-chemistry, NSF sponsored about 27 percent of the highly cited articles; for all-science-citing-chemistry, NSF sponsorship was about 15 percent. Use the quartile partitioning plus sponsor-identification sampling method to generate such estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify institutional type of performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize the institution of performing investigators using institutional-type abbreviations: A = academic institutions, G = government labs/FFRDCs, I = industry, F = foreign institutions, NP = nonprofit institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories when tabulating where innovations were performed and when analyzing relationships between institution type and funding/support patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify relationship of funding to innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Define categories for the relationship of funding to an innovation: D = direct (an explicit and direct reference to the expected advance in the proposal), G = general (broadly defined programs of research in the general area of the innovation), I = indirect (related neither directly nor generally to the justification for the funds used), NA = not available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these categories to determine whether funding was specifically aimed at supporting the innovation, broadly related, or unrelated—useful for assessing whether funding was instrumental in producing the innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record prior funding source categories (graduate fellowship, grant, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Track and report prior NSF or other funding types (e.g., GE = graduate fellowship, G = grant) when compiling innovation histories and support analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include prior funding in tables and histories to characterize investigators' funding backgrounds and to relate prior support to later innovations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proposal submission and success ratios to assess young scientist support
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure proposal submission counts and success ratios for young versus established investigators (e.g., number and percent of proposals submitted by young investigators and changes over time) to evaluate opportunities available to young scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation caveats: proposal counts underestimate total support because many young scientists work under umbrella grants, as coinvestigators, or in institute programs. Observed declines in young-investigator proposals (e.g., chemistry: from 29% of proposals in 1970 to 23% in 1975) may reflect reduced expectations of success. Use multiple data sources (surveys, awardee age distributions) to triangulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey reviewer perceptions of peer-review bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and report reviewer perceptions (e.g., whether peer review favors well-established PIs over not-yet-established PIs) as a metric of perceived fairness in the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stratified reporting (by academic generation, region, institution type) to detect patterns in perceptions; supplement perception data with objective measures (age of awardees, success ratios) because perceptions may not match outcome data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare age distribution of awardees to population to detect aging
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the age (or career age) distribution of funded principal investigators with that of the general academic doctoral population to assess whether awardees are older (i.e., whether the funded population is aging faster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example findings: small samplings found NSF-funded PIs tend to be older and more senior in rank than the general academic science population; use longitudinal comparisons (e.g., 1972 vs 1974) and cross-field studies to validate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use limited-scope, field-specific analyses when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When resources limit full examination, choose fields with manageable item counts for deeper validation (e.g., chemistry chosen due to smaller number of items and lower cost of contacting principal investigators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field-specific analyses can provide quicker validation of methods (e.g., comparing once-mentioned items to twice-or-more-mentioned items) but be cautious in generalizing beyond the chosen field.
